walkthrough:
Read the Two Optima**
Both curves rise to a peak then fall, which is the normal enzyme temperature pattern. False flax peaks earlier at about $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ with activity about 0.117-0.118 arbitrary units. Cotton peaks later at about $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ with activity about 0.102-0.104 arbitrary units.

Compare Height and Range**
So cotton has the higher optimum temperature, but false flax has the higher maximum activity. Cotton is also more heat tolerant - its curve continues to about $42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$, while false flax drops to near zero by about $37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Use the Crossover to Make Paired Comparisons**
The curves cross at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ where both are about 0.104 au. That gives you a neat paired statement: at temperatures below $30^{\circ}\text{C}$, for example at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, flax is higher (0.112 vs 0.098). At temperatures above $30^{\circ}\text{C}$, for example at $35^{\circ}\text{C}$, cotton is higher (0.093 vs 0.050). Always quote temperature, both values and units.

Add a Similarity**
For full compare credit include what is the same: both activities increase with temperature to an optimum then decrease due to denaturation, and both have identical activity at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: Cotton has higher optimum temp ~$30^{\circ}\text{C}$ vs false flax ~$25^{\circ}\text{C}$; peak activity higher in false flax ~0.118 au vs cotton ~0.103 au; cotton functions to higher temp up to ~$42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ vs flax to ~$37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$; below $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ flax activity higher than cotton, above $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ cotton higher; both increase then decrease; both ~0.104 au at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$. Any four points.

hints: Think about where these two crops grow - if one enzyme works best at hotter temperatures, what does that tell you about its habitat?
Remember all enzymes are proteins coded for by DNA - what level of difference between the two species could produce different enzymes?
Link the DNA difference to protein structure - how would a change in amino acid sequence affect stability at high temperature?
walkthrough:
Adaptation to Habitat**
Cotton, Gossypium hirsutum, grows in hotter parts of the world than false flax. Natural selection has favoured forms of rubisco activase that keep working at higher leaf temperatures in cotton.

Genetic Basis**
The two species have different base sequences in the gene for rubisco activase - different genes or different alleles. That means the mRNA and then the polypeptide will be different.

From Primary to Tertiary Structure**
A different sequence of amino acids is a different primary structure. That changes how the chain folds, so hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bridges form in different places. The result is a different tertiary structure with a different shape of active site and different resistance to disruption by heat, so optimum temperature and denaturation temperature differ.

Final answer: Cotton adapted to / grows in higher temperature regions than false flax; different genes / alleles code for rubisco activase in the two species; giving different amino acid sequence / primary structure; leading to different tertiary structure / bonds and different thermal stability / optimum.

hints: Start with what rubisco actually does in the stroma - what two molecules does it join together in the first step of the Calvin cycle?
Follow the cycle forward - if that first product GP is not made, what cannot happen next to make TP?
Think about the cycle as a cycle - if no TP is made, what happens to regeneration of the starting acceptor and to final yield?
walkthrough:
Loss of Carboxylation**
Rubisco catalyses fixation of $\text{CO}_2$ by combining $\text{CO}_2$ with the 5-carbon acceptor RuBP to form two molecules of 3-carbon GP. When heat denatures rubisco, hydrogen and other bonds break, the active site loses its specific shape, so RuBP and $\text{CO}_2$ can no longer bind. Carboxylation stops.

No GP to TP Flow**
Normally GP is phosphorylated by ATP and reduced by NADPH from the light-dependent reactions to form TP (triose phosphate). With little or no GP formed, little or no TP is produced.

Cycle Stalls and Yield Falls**
Some TP is normally used to regenerate RuBP, using more ATP, and the rest is used to make glucose, amino acids and other products. With no TP, RuBP cannot be regenerated so the cycle cannot continue, and no glucose or other carbohydrate is made for growth and yield.
Final answer: Less / no carboxylation of RuBP / fixation of $\text{CO}_2$; less / no GP reduced to TP; less / no regeneration of RuBP; less / no glucose / hexose / carbohydrate made.

hints: Look back at Fig. 2.1 - which plant already has the heat-tolerant version of rubisco activase that keeps rubisco working above $37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$?
To give that advantage to a heat-sensitive crop, what molecule carrying that trait must be moved, and what will it allow at high temperature?
walkthrough:
Move the Heat-Stable Gene**
Fig. 2.1 shows cotton rubisco activase still works at $35-42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ when false flax activase has almost stopped. Take the gene or cDNA coding for cotton rubisco activase and insert it by genetic engineering into cells or embryos of false flax or another heat-sensitive crop.

Explain the Benefit**
The transgenic crop will now make cotton-type activase as well as, or instead of, its own. That activase keeps rubisco in its active form at high environmental temperatures, so $\text{CO}_2$ fixation, the Calvin cycle and photosynthesis continue and the plant can grow and give good yield in heat.

Final answer: Isolate gene / cDNA for cotton rubisco activase and insert into false flax / heat-sensitive crop; transgenic plants produce heat-stable activase so rubisco stays active at high temps / $>37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ up to $42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$, maintaining Calvin cycle and yield.
